# Kill the Carried Interest Loophole First. Here Is What "First" Really Takes.

*Opinion and analysis, with reported facts cited inline. Anything I could not source is marked **[UNSOURCED]**. A sourcing note at the end explains what was and wasn't verified.*

*This piece does not report or rely on any specific election result. Everything below depends on who actually holds the House, the Senate and the White House when the new Congress starts, so read the "if" statements as real ifs.*

---

## The loophole in one minute

Hedge fund and private equity managers usually get paid in two ways: a fee for running the fund, and a cut of the profits, called **carried interest**. The fee is taxed like a salary. The profit cut is taxed at the lower rate for long-term investment gains, even though the manager is being paid for their work, not for putting in their own money. That's why critics call it a loophole.

The size of the gap is large. Under the 2022 Democratic bill, a related short-term gain could be taxed [at as much as 37%](https://bisnow.com/national/news/economy/sen-sinema-to-play-pivotal-role-on-fate-of-carried-interest-114182), while [long-term capital gains max out at 20%](https://www.mondaq.com:443/unitedstates/venture-capital/1237800/survival-of-the-carried-interest-reform-to-the-private-equity-model-has-been-voted-away-again) for high earners.

Congress did touch it once. The 2017 tax law added [Section 1061, which requires a three-year holding period](https://www.ncbarblog.com/?p=33017) before carried interest gets the lower rate. Critics say that was [not a sweeping change](https://taxnotes.com/tax-reform/carrying-carried-interest), and one trade-press summary notes that private equity deals often run [longer than three years anyway](https://frostbrowntodd.com/how-new-irc-1061-impacts-carried-interests), which blunts the rule's effect on them.

[UNSOURCED] The common description of fund pay as "2 and 20" (a 2% fee plus a 20% profit share) is general industry knowledge I did not verify from a retrieved source.

## What actually happened in 2022

Your memory is basically right, with one detail worth fixing.

The provision was not voted down. It was **removed before the vote** as the price of one senator's support. Sinema announced she would back the Inflation Reduction Act after [an agreement to remove the carried interest provision](https://www.necn.com/news/business/money-report/schumer-says-sinema-left-no-choice-but-to-cut-carried-interest-provision-from-tax-and-climate-bill/2799804/). The version that was dropped would have [extended the short-term rate treatment to five years](https://www.necn.com/news/business/money-report/schumer-says-sinema-left-no-choice-but-to-cut-carried-interest-provision-from-tax-and-climate-bill/2799804/) and was projected to raise about $14 billion over ten years. Schumer said she [told him she wouldn't vote to begin debate](https://news.yahoo.com/schumer-defends-dropping-carried-interest-175218755.html?fr=sycsrp_catchall) with it in the bill, and he replaced the lost money with a stock-buyback excise tax projected at [$74 billion](https://news.yahoo.com/schumer-defends-dropping-carried-interest-175218755.html?fr=sycsrp_catchall).

Her vote was decisive because Democrats had no spare votes. She was [the 50th Democrat and the clinching vote](https://thebadgerproject.org/2025/05/27/baldwin-other-dems-ask-trump-to-ditch-wall-street-tax-break-in-big-gop-bill/), and the bill passed [51-50](https://www.mondaq.com:443/unitedstates/venture-capital/1237800/survival-of-the-carried-interest-reform-to-the-private-equity-model-has-been-voted-away-again) (the 51st vote being the vice president's).

Notice what that means. The loophole survived not because 60 senators protected it, but because **one** senator out of 50 did. That is the whole story of this tax break: it doesn't need a majority. It needs one reliable holdout in the right seat.

## You're right about the filibuster. Mostly.

Tax bills can move through **budget reconciliation**, a fast-track process where [debate is limited to twenty hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconciliation_(United_States_Congress)) and [a simple majority is enough](https://www.ncsl.org/resources/details/how-the-congressional-reconciliation-process-works), so no filibuster. That is how the 2022 bill passed.

But "no filibuster" is not "no obstacles":

- **You need a budget resolution first.** Congress [must first pass a budget resolution](https://www.americanactionforum.org/research/budget-reconciliation-primer/) that unlocks the process.
- **The Byrd rule applies.** The Senate parliamentarian can strike provisions with [incidental or no budgetary effect](https://cof.org/content/budget-reconciliation). A tax change that raises money is on firmer ground than most, though the parliamentarian's call is never guaranteed. [UNSOURCED] My view that carried interest would likely pass the Byrd test is an inference, not a ruling.
- **The president still signs or vetoes.** [Congress can override a veto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconciliation_(United_States_Congress)) only with two-thirds of both chambers.
- **One vehicle per budget resolution.** One summary notes that [a budget resolution can only provide for one reconciliation bill](https://cof.org/content/budget-reconciliation), so Congress has historically used it to [package the majority's priorities together](https://cof.org/content/budget-reconciliation).

That last point is the catch in "do this first." Reconciliation is scarce. Spending your one shot on a roughly $14 billion item (the 2022 estimate for a five-year version; a different design would score differently) is a choice, not a freebie.

## "Now" means January

There is no "now." The Constitution ends the current Congress at noon on January 3. [The 119th Congress ends and the 120th begins on January 3, 2027](https://protectdemocracy.org/work/how-does-congress-seat-election-winners/). Until then, [Republicans retain control](https://www.legal500.com/intelligence/united-states/government-public-sector/lame-duck-high-stakes-congress%E2%80%99s-postelection-agenda) of the chambers they currently hold. So nothing you want can pass on the strength of last night's results. The earliest real action is the new Congress.

And the senator in question is gone. Sinema [officially left office on January 3, 2025](https://www.advocate.com/politics/kyrsten-sinema-funds-misuse-complaint), when Ruben Gallego was sworn in, after she [announced in March 2024](https://www.eenews.net/articles/sinema-wont-run-for-reelection/) she wouldn't run again. The lesson is not "she's gone, problem solved." Any caucus with a thin majority has a pivotal vote somewhere. Whoever that is, find out who is wooing them.

## The part nobody likes: the White House

Here's the twist. This is not purely a left-versus-right fight.

- Trump called the loophole ["ridiculous" in 2016](https://thebadgerproject.org/2025/05/27/baldwin-other-dems-ask-trump-to-ditch-wall-street-tax-break-in-big-gop-bill/), and the 2017 law he signed only [added the three-year holding requirement](https://thebadgerproject.org/2025/05/27/baldwin-other-dems-ask-trump-to-ditch-wall-street-tax-break-in-big-gop-bill/).
- In 2025 the administration [announced it would seek to close it](https://www.mondaq.com/unitedstates/capital-gains-tax/1587574/tax-proposals-bid-adieu-to-carried-interest), and Republican Sen. Josh Hawley [said "They ought to close the carried interest loophole"](https://www.yahoo.com/news/not-done-yet-us-senate-190612860.html) during the debate over Trump's big tax bill.
- It didn't happen. Reporting at the time said the Senate version [did not end the loophole](https://www.denvergazette.com/?p=76927), and the industry's resistance had [killed other recent attempts](https://www.westhawaiitoday.com/?p=283510).

So a president who has said he supports it, in public, repeatedly, still didn't get it done when he had a unified Congress. [UNSOURCED] I did not find a current, on-the-record statement of his position from this fall, so I can't tell you whether he would sign or veto a bill today.

Democrats have also not been consistent. They introduced a new bill, the [Ending the Carried Interest Loophole Act](https://www.dlapiper.com/en-ma/insights/publications/2026/05/carried-interest-reform-returns-to-congress), in April 2026 from Sens. Wyden, Whitehouse and King. It would repeal Section 1061 and replace it with [a deemed-compensation framework that creates annual "phantom income"](https://www.dlapiper.com/insights/publications/2026/05/carried-interest-reform-returns-to-congress) for carried interest holders. As introduced it [has no Republican sponsors](https://www.dlapiper.com/en-cl/insights/publications/2026/05/carried-interest-reform-returns-to-congress). Its last recorded action was [referral to the Finance Committee](https://fastdemocracy.com/bill-search/us/119/bills/USB00104379/). One law-firm summary cautions the bill [only reflects proposed legislation and current law has not changed](https://www.dlapiper.com/en-cl/insights/publications/2026/05/carried-interest-reform-returns-to-congress).

## Why the fight is so hard to win

Because the people on the other side are organized and the people on your side are not.

Fox News reported that Sinema [raised significant campaign money from the private equity sector](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/sinema-top-private-equity-cash-recipients-removed-billionaire-tax-loophole-manchin-bill) around the time she pushed to remove the provision, and the Chamber of Commerce [applauded her effort](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/sinema-top-private-equity-cash-recipients-removed-billionaire-tax-loophole-manchin-bill). The New Republic reported she'd collected [$2.2 million from the financial sector since 2017](https://newrepublic.com/article/167318/kyrsten-hedge-funds-inflation-reduction-act-carried-interest-tax-loophole) and called much of it "a likely payoff." **That "payoff" claim is the author's opinion, not proof.** Donations and votes can line up for reasons other than a trade. Sinema herself had said before that [ending the loophole could undermine competitiveness](https://bisnow.com/national/news/economy/sen-sinema-to-play-pivotal-role-on-fate-of-carried-interest-114182), a view some economists and the industry share.

Still, the pattern is hard to ignore. A tax rule that [most experts call indefensible](https://www.democracyrenovator.com/p/the-carried-interest-loophole-is) has [survived at least half a dozen challenges](https://www.democracyrenovator.com/p/the-carried-interest-loophole-is) and [outlasted four presidents](https://www.democracyrenovator.com/p/the-carried-interest-loophole-is), per one business-school commentator writing in October. That's a column, so treat "most experts" as his characterization. Even so, the list of people who've said it should be taxed as ordinary income [reportedly includes Warren Buffett, Robert Rubin and Peter Orszag](https://www.democracyrenovator.com/p/the-carried-interest-loophole-is).

## My argument

Here is the case for your plan, and the case against it, in plain terms.

**For doing it first.** It is a test. A party that says it will tax the powerful and then protects a rule that lets money managers pay a lower rate than many of the people who clean their offices has a credibility problem. Passing it early, over industry objections, shows the promises are real. It's also easy to explain: same work, same tax.

**Against doing it first.** It's small money. If reconciliation is scarce, a $14 billion item might be better as one piece of a larger package than as a standalone. And "first" only works if the votes are actually there. A failed or watered-down vote is worse than waiting, because it teaches the industry that the threat is empty.

**What I'd actually do.** Treat it as a loyalty test for your own caucus before the vote, not after. Whip the count in advance. Publish who's undecided. Make the 2022 story the opening line: one senator held it up, and everyone knew her name. If you can't name the 50th vote before you introduce the bill, you're not ready, whatever the order of operations.

And find Republican allies like Hawley now, not later. If the White House has said it's for this, make it prove it with a signature.

## Sourcing note

**Verified from retrieved sources (secondary reporting, law-firm and trade summaries):** the 2022 removal of the provision as the price of Sinema's support; the $14B and $74B projections; the 51-50 vote; the 2017 three-year holding period; the reconciliation rules (simple majority, 20-hour debate, budget resolution, Byrd rule, veto); the January 3, 2027 start of the next Congress and continued control by the current majority until then; Sinema's departure in January 2025; the April 2026 Wyden/Whitehouse/King bill and its committee referral.

**Secondary sources I'd verify before publishing:** the 37% vs. 20% rate comparison (drawn from a law-firm bulletin, and the 37% figure refers to short-term treatment); the claim that carried interest is taxed mainly as long-term gain (supported generally, but I didn't pull an IRS or CRS primary document); the Whitehouse, Wyden and King bill's mechanics (from a law-firm summary, not the bill text). A third-party article claims the bill would raise rates to as high as 40.8%, which I did not independently verify and did not rely on.

**Contested or opinion:** whether donations "paid off" a vote; whether the industry's competitiveness argument is correct; whether the five-year holding period would "effectively repeal" the loophole (an opinion in a magazine piece I chose not to repeat as fact).

**Flagged as unsourced in the text:** the "2 and 20" description; my inference about the Byrd rule; Trump's current position.

**Not primary documents:** I did not retrieve the 2022 Senate roll call, the Joint Committee on Taxation score, the bill text, or an IRS document. Those would be the next step before publication.

**Excluded:** a prediction-market page and an anonymous "do not publish" law-firm draft turned up in searches. I did not rely on either.

**Not covered:** I did not report election results, per the request. The article is conditional on what the results turn out to mean for the January majorities.
